content: After abdominal surgeries, including caesarean sections, it is a common practice to withhold oral fluids and food for a certain period. However, practices regarding the timing of reintroducing oral intake after caesarean sections vary significantly, raising questions about the rationale behind these differing approaches. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of introducing oral fluids and/or food early versus delaying their introduction after caesarean sections. The review included clinical trials that randomly assigned women to either early or delayed oral intake within the first 24 hours post-surgery. The definition of early feeding was determined by the individual trial authors, typically within six to eight hours after the procedure. The studies included in the review were assessed for their methodological quality and suitability for inclusion. For binary outcomes, relative risks and 95% confidence intervals were calculated, while continuous outcomes were analyzed using weighted mean differences and 95% confidence intervals. Subgroup analyses were conducted based on the type of anesthesia used (general, regional, or mixed/undefined). Out of 12 studies considered, six were included in the review, while four were excluded, and two are awaiting further information. The quality of the included studies varied, and only a small number of studies provided usable data for each outcome. Three studies focused exclusively on surgeries performed under regional anesthesia, while the other three included both regional and general anesthesia. The findings suggested that early oral intake was associated with several benefits: A shorter time to the first food intake (based on one study involving 118 women, where a slush diet was introduced according to clinical parameters; the weighted mean difference was -7.20 hours, with a 95% confidence interval of -13.26 to -1.14). A reduced time to the return of bowel sounds (one study, 118 women; weighted mean difference of -4.30 hours, with a 95% confidence interval of -6.78 to -1.82). A shorter postoperative hospital stay following surgery under regional anesthesia (two studies, 220 women; weighted mean difference of -0.75 days, with a 95% confidence interval of -1.37 to -0.12, using a random-effects model). A trend toward reduced abdominal distension (three studies, 369 women; relative risk of 0.78, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.55 to 1.11). However, no significant differences were observed between early and delayed oral intake in terms of nausea, vomiting, time to bowel action or passing flatus, incidence of paralytic ileus, or the number of analgesic doses required. The authors concluded that there is no evidence from the limited randomized trials reviewed to support a policy of withholding oral fluids after uncomplicated caesarean sections. They emphasized the need for further research to better inform clinical practice.
